whatItDoes: Estimates the capital gain or loss from selling an asset. It subtracts purchase price and any buying/selling costs, then applies the tax rate you enter to the taxable gain to show the estimated tax owed.
whyItExists: Selling an asset — stock, property, or crypto — creates a gain that is often taxed, but the taxable profit depends on the exact costs of buying and selling. A quick calculator makes the real, net gain and its tax easy to see.
whoShouldUse: Investors selling stocks or funds, property owners, and anyone planning a sale where a capital gain tax applies.
useCases: Estimate tax on a stock or mutual fund sale
Budget for a property sale with closing costs
Compare scenarios of different cost assumptions
See whether a sale is actually with gain or loss
Plan the timing of a sale across tax years
Check how higher purchase costs change the taxable gain
instructions: Enter the purchase price of the asset
Add any selling costs (agent fees, closing costs)
Enter the tax rate and read the estimated gain and tax
Adjust the rate to model long-term vs. short-term holdings
examples: Purchased $50,000 + $500 fees, sold $75,000 − $1,000 fees, 15% rate → gain $23,500, tax ≈ $3,525
Purchased $20,000, sold $15,000 → a $5,000 loss, no taxable gain, no tax
Purchased $10,000 + $200 fees, sold $18,000 − $300 fees, 20% rate → gain $7,500, tax ≈ $1,500
Same gain held short-term at 32% → tax rises to ≈ $2,400, showing why holding period matters
bestPractices: Include all fees — commissions, closing, legal, transfer taxes
Use the correct rate for your holding period (long-term vs short-term)
Check the current tax authority rates before relying on the figure
Treat the number as an estimate, not tax advice
Track your basis documents so purchase costs are accurate
commonMistakes: Forgetting purchase or selling costs that reduce the gain
Applying the tax rate to the full sale price instead of the gain
Ignoring that losses usually mean no tax is owed
Assuming one flat rate applies to every situation
Mixing up long-term and short-term holding periods
faq: Is this tax advice? — No, it is an informational estimate based on the inputs.
What if I sold at a loss? — The loss is shown and the taxable gain is zero.
Which rate should I use? — Use the rate applicable to your asset: long-term, short-term, or local rules.
Are my numbers shared? — No, the calculation is done entirely in your browser.
What is the difference between long-term and short-term? — Most tax systems tax assets held over one year at a lower rate than those sold within a year.
Can I offset gains with losses? — Yes, in many systems capital losses reduce taxable gains; enter a net figure to model it.
